I have been a silent reader of this forum for several months and decided to start a Journal and begin contributing to this wonderful community. I'd like to thank IF for offering this place to those of us who are committed to understanding how and why the market moves like it does. I am immensely thankful for the time and continued efforts all associate and master traders who take the time to respond to those of us who are still in the beginning stages of our journey to becoming competent traders.

I found this website in August 2014 and joined November 2014. Despite not posting any content to date, I have spent at least an hour a day going through the homework assignments and member journals in my quest to understand price movement. Previous to finding RTM last year I spent two arduous years trading Forex with little success. This community has helped tremendously.

I have read through all of the materials posted under the Marketpedia section (multiple times) and after reading through various Journals over several months I feel the following concepts are most important when it comes to truly understanding how everything fits together: It has something to do with the relationship between:

1. How to accurately draw all price action zones and understand the difference between an engulf and a fakeout. 2. Proficiency in using multiple time frames to utilize the fractal nature of the market to pinpoint critical reaction levels and decision points.

Aaron's 'Homework Room' topic titled 'Engulf or Fakeout?' has been a great resource that has helped me see the difference between an engulf/fakeout. Many thanks to him for starting that thread!

For me, drawing the PAZ is the most challenging concept to understand and draw accurately. My goal is to finally take each article from the Marketpedia section and begin combining the concepts together to see the bigger picture behind price movement. This journal will be a great place to begin this journey, post my charts, and track my progress.

I plan on posting both historical chart analysis (hindsight) for conceptual purposes as well as live trades taken on a demo account for practical application and accountability. I will perform a 'trade autopsy' on any live trades I take that fail so I can identify the mistakes and eliminate bad habits.

First chart posted here is just for practice to make sure I am inserting the picture correctly. I am using Gyazo to snap screenshots.

More posts to follow...

Trade Setup – Hindsight: I found a nice example of an AUD/USD FTB reaction that took place back on 6/2/15. This is not a trade I caught in real time but one I researched in hindsight to see if I could identify why price reacted like it did.

HTF Analysis: This is a good area to look for a reaction on the FTB because the associated FTR is significant. There is a clear decision made that price is too expensive and a resulting price cap is formed. There is a strong bearish move out of the FTR showing a significant imbalance where more orders may exist when price returns to this area. Because of these factors, I will watch the 4-hour chart until price reaches the FTR zone, at which point I will drop down to a LTF to look for specific price action to make an entry.

LTF Analysis: Price moves up through the lower limit of the FTR. Since I know price is returning for the first time, I am looking for a reason to short. Primarily, I am focused on price forming an engulf to the downside before considering any entry. This is not a situation where I would risk a TT.

In this example, price does end up engulfing and in doing so also forms the LL of the QM.

I labeled the source of the engulf as the location where I would have executed a short trade. I would have placed a stop just above the upper limit of the FTR (around.78420). Target is shown on chart. My target might be a little aggressive, and there’s a good chance I would have taken ½ of the position off around.76940 just to be safe.

Fakeout vs Engulf: It’s my understanding that price will fakeout when IT’s needs orders. Fakeouts are used to push price in to a specific zone that will contain orders. Engulfs and fakeouts both have the same effect on retail traders (tricks), but the engulf is really just indicative of future price direction. Because of this, engulfs usually don’t engulf in to a significant level. That is why I think this example shows an engulf and not a F/O.

This is an example on EUR/GBP (4-HR Chart) where compression exists between two FTR’s. My focus is on the location of the engulf and the subsequent final bullish push through the CP in to the FTR zone above (by the large black arrow).

Was there a way I could have predicted that price would reach the upper FTR following the bearish engulf?

I am not entirely sure how to read this chart accurately. On one hand, the engulf on the 4-hour chart could be read as a clear intention for price to drop. In this were case, the IT’s would need to fill lots of short orders. Since the lower FTR zone is depleted (three times price has visited this FTR), it would make logical sense that price would need to find the next real level of Supply to fill short orders. The push through the CP to the upper FTR could be seen as a FTB, but it also looks like a great place to FO and load up on short orders.

Maybe this is both a FTB and a FO?

IF’s trades often occur at levels where he experiences very little (if any) drawdown. After breaking down some of those amazing trades I notice many times he is able to predict in advance and place a PO at the exact area where price turns.

I could be wrong, but it seems like he knows where the fakeouts will occur by looking left of the engulf to see what the RBD/ DBR (supply/demand) is reacting to (usually an important FTR) and determining whether there are any extreme orders left to fill in that FTR. If so, price will likely FO to a specific decision point within this FTR. That is why he often drop down to a 5 minute or 1 minute chart to plot his entry….he is looking for the most accurate decision point.

This is what I need to work on because trading at these extreme levels offers the highest R:R.

Away

Hi Gembel,

Thank you for pointing out the obvious engulf I missed! I have a bad habit of seeing what I want to see on a chart and missing important zones. It's easy to immediately form a bias from looking at a chart without thoroughly analyzing all the important zones and engulfs. Also, thank you for drawing the CP PAZ...I need to practice drawing those.

One of my worst habits is being overly anxious to get in a trade out of fear that I'll miss an opportunity. It's a completely irrational fear, as any trader knows there are dozens of prime setups that occur every day. That said, I still regularly fall victim to this and it happened this evening on a trade I took on the Cable. Here are the charts (1-HR and 1-Min)

I saw price bounce from a HTF FTR, so I dropped down to a 1-minute chart to see price action. The 1-minute chat showed a nice engulf and bearish QM setup so I waited for price to retrace to the origin of the engulf and took a short trade. My stop was a couple of pips above the swing high and my target was the base of the pole.

Here is why it went wrong:

Almost as soon as I executed the short trade I began having doubts. I looked at the 4-HR chart and saw a bullish reaction out of demand which made me question my reasons for taking short. Even though the short position was a quick scalp, I was concerned the QM was going to fail. Because of this, I closed the trade with a minimal 2.5 pip gain (barely enough to cover the spread).

Of course, within a few short minutes of closing my position, price ended up dropping to easily hit my original target. I tried to jump back in when I saw price take a dive, but was only able to pick up another 4 or 5 pips.

I am embarrassed to admit that after three years of trading I still make these kind of mistakes.

Looking forward to kicking this bad habit.

Here is a follow up from my AUD/USD Chart from last week (see Post #2 for original post on this pair).

I listed the steps (see chart) that I would take when watching price develop in to this critical level to predict a F/O. In this case, price did react nicely to this level, as it picked up the extreme set of orders still left in the original FTR. My question: it it OK that price (when forming "A") exceeded the extreme set of orders by a few pips (see the orange dotted line)? If so, why did this happen and how can I predict this happening in the future? I don't see any value in pushing price beyond the last set of orders in the FTR, unless it was done just to fool traders. Even so, this ~ 10 pip move past the extreme FTR seems arbitrary.

When IF takes his trades, he seems to know almost exactly where price will turn. While I am not expecting to trade with IF's level of accuracy, it does concern me when an extreme level (which is supposed to be a F/O) is engulfed. It makes me think I am misreading the chart.

Of course, ideally a trader would zoom in and watch for PA before taking a trade. That said, IF has many trades that he takes without waiting for price action because he is expecting the F/O and knows exactly where price will turn. This is what I am trying to understand on a conceptual level.

I dont know half as much as you I am sure, so I could be talking bollox....or not...

Price went up, broke highs, lots of buyers at supply, FO. Price sold off. There may well be a reason why price was overwhelmed in the FO tail by looking left - most probably a SR. IMO its irrelevant.

You havent highlighted the fact the FTB was a breach of a flag at SR over to the left. In reality its not any different.

Very exciting to be on a path towards understanding this better!

Thanks for the reality check and encouragement Ptp!! Maybe I am getting caught up on insignificant details (I have a tendency to obsess on details and miss the main point). Where I often struggle is stop placement - either the trades get run through or the stop gets hit just before price reverses. The difference between a winning trade and a losing trade can be stop placement.

Knowing price is going to F/O allows a trader to widen their stop and keeps them on the right side of R:R. It's amazing to see how bad timing on an otherwise excellent trade setup can take a major winner and turn it in to a loser. I am actually embarrassed at how often my stops get hit...

To improve on my past errors, I have started closely watching price to understand why price changes when it does. That's why I was surprised to see price break the extreme orders of the FTR by ten pips (AUD/USD).

IF has mentioned many times that predicting a F/O should be easy. I agree that an engulf or a F/O have basically the same effect on retail traders as far as trapping them on the wrong side of the trade (and in that context the difference between them really doesn't matter). Of course, the difference between the engulf and F/O is the engulf dictates future price direction. And I would suggest (from what I know as a beginner) that it is incredibly important to distinguish between the two from a practical perspective.

I suppose the other aspect of this that I need to work on is the PAZ. It seems simple enough in theory...PAZ is just the space between FTR's. For some reason, once I open a live chart, I start getting all mixed up on how to draw them, how to not leave any out, and how to understand price's reaction to them.

Enough of my rambling...I really appreciate that you and D took the time to leave a comment here and I will try to stay focused on the bigger picture and get really competent at specific setups that I can duplicate over and over.

You have the right attitude which is more important than any price structure. In the trade of #19, my advice is to try to avoid looking for the exact reason. Is price at a key supply/SR zone? Check. First time back? Check. If you want to, was there an engulf? Check. Now decide where to get in. If you see the RBD between the doji and the red candle, theres a clear little pullback in there - one of those "ftr" things. Its simply a pullback before the drop, and theres a level in it. That little ftr is NO DIFFERENT to a fakeout, its just within the price curve it was part of in the up move. I dont even know whats left but that push up had to react at the most obvious next reaction point, which is the FTR or whatver its called.....and to be clear, I would have been in on the RBD, not the retest, around 27722 or even around 277738. This was a really easy trade H - so if it feels like it is hard, you are possibly looking for something thats not there, or really not relevant. This trade is at major supply, and it rotates. Jump in on the rotation or wait for the engulf. If you look at the M1 chart at the PA left of the entry, what I see as being more predictive is a nice SR level around the entry. If you look at M1 the entry higher, simple SR, was a much better price. In either case you still dont know if price will rip north...thats the uncertainty principle. I personally dont like the entry that was taken - it looks good on a H1.

You have a good read on price, thats clear to see. I dont like how you use the word "trick" in some of your charts - for me that sets me up emotionally to think there are these douche bags playing the rest of retail. I have worked in the depths of the financial markets since 2006, and I have never come across this. I even looked very deeply into the notion of big players pushing price around. Price does get pushed around by big players, the shops that have the money are often huge institutions, and they arent half as clever as we are made to believe. The smarts in trading comes from the smaller places, and often they have strict risk controls. One reason prop trading is a double-edged sword is that often the way to make good money due to the split involves leverage, but it can take a long long time before the company will give you that leverage. I was offered a role at ITG as a prop trader - to learn it - and it ws impossible to survive due to the risk. Ignoring the recent big-sell side bullshit around chatting each other in FX, I do not believe that exists in the futures world....yet the same patterns unfold.

Its not a trick, its a normal manifestation of price action. It is behavioral finance made-manifest. If you see things as tricks, its difficult to not feel an emotional response when oyu are on the wrong side. I lost a lot of money on the wrong side of a spoofing in the russell 2000 last year, and it was hard not to get angry. Trading in my view is 20% setup, 80% psychology, and this is where my problems lie today. I can read price. know how to manage my trades to makea lot of money. I struggle with emotions...a common problem when trying to move into full time day trading I read.

Regardless, you will work it out, but question everything, including what you read as being "the situation" of what you are reading in price. I just see it as price doing what it does. Its helped me a lot, and I avoid anthropomorphic projections as best that I can.

PTP,

One question I've had regarding the markets is this: If the retail market makes up only a very small percentage of the total currency traded in the market (many trillions per day total), then would the IT's be trying to trap and trick retail traders? If IT's are trading on huge positions, the retail trader liquidity would not be even close to enough buying or selling power to push a position really far. Retail potions would be like one peanut to an elephant....This has always puzzled me logically.

That said, many traders (not just IT's) know where stops are likely to be located at certain places along the way. It would make sense to me that stop hunting would help fill orders...and unless I am just 'seeing what I want to see', stop hunts happen all the time. I've been caught in them countless times (I've lost a staggering amount of $ over the past couple of years due to these 'pushes' through support/resistance to a level where my stop was located only to see price snap back and end up going the direction I originally traded.

You would fall over if you knew how much money I've lost...this is why I am demo only for now.

As always, thank you for your posts and willingness to offer your knowledge!

In Market Wizards, the stop run and the understanding of placing stops at better locations to avoid getting hit by a stop run, imply the act of searching for stops. Whats not clear is, is it one program or institute, or many, and are they collaborating or not. Furthermore, when you move to the edge of a price curve, there will be a lot more emotional response/activity there than mid-curve for example, and the ability to control how far price moves can be a tricky problem. FX brokers know where your orders are and nefarious acts by them to force bad fills is a known worry of the FX space - wild wild west - certainly on the smaller timeframes. But there are many reasons why price may run past a level, all of which could be a mixture of program/retail/whoever.

Nevertheless, I play this from the perspective of these areas are merely key places where more emotion plays out and the location is less a price lvel and more a zone.

It seems clear to me that people know where stops are - pick up any book on retail trading and you can see the advice given about placing a stop at the high of an entry candle + 1 tick or so. A single candle can have breakout traders and range traders all playing out their own views of the market price action. When price reaches an extreme, a key decision has to be made, and that really in my view comes from the larger market, with some nudging from size. If price FO's the highs, the question for the bulls is, will this hold or not. If they get any indication they could be wrong, they will close the trade - there will be a panic often at the extremes, more so in more volatile instruments. Crude is a great example. It is actually pretty easy to spot the emotion watching the tape at the extremes. It might well be that "its" push price beyond a level and then they wait for the response of the market to see if price snaps back. Or they could be trying to drive price up and then back down. I can see how that would go, but market manipulation is illegal. Spoofing, a major tactic that was known/is known to exist, is illegal. Its illegal because its market manipulation.

For me at least, its better to think about emotions at various places, agnostic of nefarious activities, because I actually think regardless of the programs/bad practices that may go on, the price action would look much the same. I could be wrong, but I find that outlook allows me to at least not feel like I am being taken from behind by the investment oligarchy.

I have lost a lot of money being on the wrong side of a range play where price snaps back into the range. I once took a short on TF, the Russell 2000, and I was so cock-sure of myself I loaded up - it was a surety price was going lower. Best trading experience I ever had - I watch for that all of the time and make sure I am on the right side of it now. Explosive moves from such places. All I do now is look for similar locations for explosive moves - places I fondly refer to as High Probability Reversal Zones.

H, let me caveat this with the following. I trade a lot differently to RTM it seems (the more I look at what people do or get stuck doing here I notice how I am seeing price alot differently). My intention is day trading, and so I am looking for how to extract money on a daily basis. I look for D1 and H4 levels, but then I use other techniques to look for zones that I think could have a reaction based on simple price movement. If I see a key pullback, regardless of origins or breaks of more important places, I still watch them. I have found some of the most non-obvious areas can turn price, so I have learnt to be adaptive. In fact I developed my own method to embody uncertainty at its core and still have positive expectancy. Trading Crude and Gold for many months last year, I constantly had my @ss handed to me for making assumptions or sitting at the charts with a bias.

I should also mention I use tape, order flow, tick charts, volume charts and in some cases volume profile. I use no indicators.

I marked out some key areas that I gravitate too. I would be reading what the larger timeframe direction is and look to trade only in that direction until price hits a reversal zone. That is, never counter-trade until its in an area to be tested. It might seem boring, but after you have your live account handed back to you empty, I am ok going for uncool with-trend trades and riding them than getting the kick of choosing the right turning point for a contrarian trade. So in this daily chart I marked out key areas I would definitely have in my sights. The daily FTR you point out falls on a key SR level, and I would be all over that when price returns.

There are many more opportunities here on the H4. Right now price has pushed into the highs, and it even looks like its rolling over. As price nears the higher part of a curve, towards a new level, thats the time to look for markers that price could fall. You dont have volume in FX AFAIK and that can be a huge marker. I WOULD HIGHLY RECOMMEND GETTING YOUR ACCOUNT TO A LEVEL TO PLAY FUTURES. I have no idea why people do FX apart from the smaller lot size....futures have mini lot sizes too, though they are still more expensive than the micro lots in FX. But you get to trade cleaner PA (my judgement).

From the comments you make in your post, I can see how you are approaching the charts and my only advice would be to try not to worry too much about whether price will turn or not. If you want to touch trade, you can spend hundreds of hours trying to perfect your ability to spot the exact turning point....maybe thats doable I dont know. was pretty good at spotting amazing turning points, when price turned, and I quickly overlooked the many more times I failed at it. Theres nothing great about selling into a zone due to an expectation of a fall only to see price rip right past your SL. The touch trade technique can work and can be easy, as long as the math works out. I found for me my ability to forecast was forever failing me. It is only made harder when you see a fantastic equity curve from an academy student, whether or not that student already had excellent success before the course or not...fear and greed....it gets us all.

My style is profoundly adaptive. I have learnt to read the market at the zones - that is where my market reading kicks in. Until then I merely mark areas I *think* will react. In your charts, if you only want to trade the higher timeframes then the locations you put out there are those that I would monitor, looking for key SR lines. SR helps me zone in, and then I will look for pullbacks on tick charts. Almost every pullback will get a reaction, but some will be deeper, and some will be reversals, while others will involve a stop out if you dont bother to listen to what the market is telling you. As long as you factor in MM into the process, the stop outs should be irrelevant. For me I can often get in on every reaction of a rotation in price at a key level, and I never know which one will be "the one" that will cause the best/true reversal. I factor this into my approach so that I frankly dont give a damn. I can mark the levels up in a matter of minutes, because to me my edge comes from rolling my sleeves up as price approaches them. Sr levels are debunked in the academy, but they offer a much simpler mechanism in my view. Theres nothing more disappointing than spending hours at the charts marking out all of the constructs based on the "rules", only to see all of them fail. My emotional constitution isnt mature enough for that.

I would conclude with this - it is a well known fact that a method that is complex is most probably riddled with a number of emotional problems. For example, when a trader who gets off with indicators takes a big hit in the market, he/she will go in search of a better indicator that will give more edge, and they will add that to their system ad nauseum, creating a more complex system. Someone else with price aciton might create a colorful and complicated way to read price action, full of all and sundry. Most of the constructs added are products of emotional distress - loss avoidance techniques. They dont exist because they are necessary to trade, but because they offer the ability for the creator to feel less emotional pain (hope for). The cosmic joke for traders is that it is profoundly simpler than we make it out to be, often because its always about trying to avoid the innate fear of loss. Most often the person who has a complicated way of trading trades little - an phenomena I found myself doing whenever I get wrapped up in complexity. My experience now is that it is simple.

I openly admit my issue is not one of price reading any longer. I struggle with the emotional/psychology side and I have a coach helping. In fact I have a bit of the Jonah Complex going on which I never thought I would have. I mention this only to highlight that my approach is extremely simple, and when I trade now I make more money than I ever thought I could. The gravity of that has been a cause for my recent need to grow psychology....but I approach the markets extremely and profoundly simply...

HTH

Hey hoeschec here are a few things to consider regarding your loss. We always have to be aware of what price is doing in all TFs. While price can certainly move up from the point you took your trade you should realize that price is coming down from supply, and the best place to buy is at a fresh demand FTR. No matter what TF you use for entry it should be backed up by and at HTF FL/FTR. Your trade was in "no mans land" on the HTF.

I certainly see your reason for the trade and it does look enticing. Price did engulf an FTR, but unfortunately it also immediately hit an important FL and the target. Its important because it is supply that engulfed and formed at the last demand. You found a place that would bounce price, but the move away from price tells you whether to keep it and discard it and try again at a better place. In this case price cp'd away which leaves no demand levels left to "guard" your entry. What you want to see is an engulf of the immediate supply/demand. Price ended up forming a QM against you. You can't see this in real time, but can see the environment in which one can form if you keep in mind all TFs and what FLs are in play on each.

This is my take.

Hi Peter,

This is a relatively new concept for me, so hopefully a more experienced trader can step in and correct me if I am wrong...but here is my understanding of what I mean by 'source' engulf.

When price is reaching an important HTF supply or demand zone, I drop down to a lower time frame to see how price forms as it reaches in to the area of importance. On its way in to the zone, price will FL many times (base-pole-flag...etc). FTR's will also form & I watch for these as well. What I look for is the original FL or FTR that acts as the source of the major push up in to the HTF zone. I also look for major S/R levels to mark the FTR that forms after the break of the S/R level. Basically, I want to find the FL or FTR that is important...not just FL's that form as a result of the important FL's. It is critical to find out which FL/FTR is the origin of the move in to the HTF zone because it is this FL/FTR that matters when it comes to a possible. engulf.

Previously, I would be watching the charts and point out what I thought was an engulf, when in reality all I was looking at was price breaking the high/low of a reactionary FL or (meaning nothing of importance happened). Here is a illustration I made a few pages back in my journal that I think is correct (nobody corrected me on it) and it does a decent job of illustrating this point.

As you can see on the illustrated chart, the original FL/FTR (arrow 1) is the one that occurred on the very Left.This is the FL/FTR that formed after a break of an important S/R level...because of this, I would deem this FTR/FL as being important and the 'source/original' FL/FTR. You can see from this drawing that price attempts to break the original FL/FTR (arrow 2) but isn't able to. Look at Arrow 3: This arrow breaks the top limit of the RBD that formed at arrow 2 making it appear that an engulf has occurred when it hasn't.

The true engulf only occurs when price is able to break the top limit of the FL/FTR show at arrow #1. The engulf happens at arrow # 4. This is confirmation that the last orders have been taken from the initial source FL/FTR and price will move to the north after (hopefully) retracing to the origin of the engulf.

This is my best understanding of the concept, and although it is hard to put in to words, I hope this drawing helps. For anyone who reads this and finds flaws in my response to Peter: please let me know! I'd hate to lead another trader down the wrong path!

Hope this help Peter, please let me know if you still don't understand that concept and I'll draw a new diagram with more examples

Since I'm sitting here bored as my Broker has temporarily closed out the platform for maintenance, I spent some time to draw out a recent concept I've been working on. Here is my interpretation of what it looks like:

1. Find a Base-Pole-Flag: where the Flag portion forms in a HTF supply or demand zone (the HTF confirmation is very important)

2. Once price starts flagging, drop down to a lower time frame and start marking out the FL's and FTR's that price makes as it spends time in your HTF supply or demand zone.

3. Mark the important FL or FTR that supports price's move in to the HTF zone and marks the end of the 'Pole' and starts the FL (this is the important FL that you want to see price engulf before looking for a place to get short).

4. Price will move sideways for a while while it consolidates. Just be patient...wait for the engulf.

5. After the engulf has occurred, start looking for a place to get short.

6. Find the high limit of the FL that formed within the HTF supply zone and watch for the area in the FL where the last orders (most extreme orders) could possibly exist. This is the MPL (I think).

7. Wait for the deep retrace to this MPL and get short with a tight stop. These entries are the ones that can be 1:10 R:R or more.

I am not sure if my drawing is 100% accurate, but I will use this idea in my trading next week to refine my entries and find trading opportunities that have a higher R:R.

Yes, there is seemingly an engulf at the blue circle (as you have pointed out). Bu the only reason we see that as an engulf is because it broke the high of the FL in the orange circle. Also, price action can form what appears to be an engulf when price is really only bouncing off a S/R flip level. I suppose we would have to look left and see why price engulfed to the upside in the red circle to find out if the break of that high ended in a critical location where orders were remaining. I think the engulf tends to take place in areas of low significance, whereas fake outs are essentially the IT's searching for LQ by triggering stops and finding pockets where orders reside.

My understanding is that an engulf might not be a true engulf if the following situations exist:

1. The potential engulf occurs at a flag that is a reaction to the original flag. 2. The potential engulf occurs at a S/R level 3. The Engulf hits its target straightaway (easy to miss if you don't look closely)

I am not trying to be pessimistic...but sometimes we share too many situations where engulfs work out and fail to take a hard look at the ones that don't, or assume that an engulf is valid just because price followed through the way we suspected it would. Lately, I've been challenging myself to look objectively at these trades and avoid a type of 'confirmation bias' where I only see the winning trades as proof that I'm understanding a concept while discounting all the evidence that points to the contrary.I am not challenging the RTM concepts, I am questioning whether I understand the concepts as well as I think I do.

It seems that everything at RTM revolves around the engulf, so it is worth the time to really practice and understand how and why they form, and how to spot them in real time - not just in retrospect looking at historic charts.

E/J Example - nice price structure with an engulf that looks pretty straightforward and clean to me...no S/R levels or reactionary flags to worry about. I see two consecutive downside engulfs, which (in my experience) increases the odds that price will follow through accordingly.

Something I have been noticing, is price often times does not RT to the origin of the engulf - many times it only retraces to the S/R flip directly above the engulf. This chart is a perfect example of the PA I see on a regular basis.

In this case, two trades could be taken: one at the S/R flip and another at the origin of the engulf (in case price does return). The downside to this strategy is the location of the stop loss - it hurts the R:R ratio substantially. So after doing more homework, here is where I am at:

1. Flag limits look exactly like FTR's to me...

2. There are crucial decision points within all of these flag limits, and they are formed as a RBD or DBR. These RBD/DBR also have base/pole/flag price forms. You have to go to the LTF to see it.

3. MPL's probably have a lot to do with wanting to achieve the best price within the flag.

4. Analogy: It seems to me that the flag is a battlefield and the flag limits represent the opposing army, defending their positions. In the case of the market, these armies are the bulls and the bears. Price must defeat the bull army or the bear army before breaking out of a flag and advancing on. The decision points are the "last stand".

Would I be right in saying the following:

Every Flag that forms must have have two flag limits. Those flag limits are formed when an engulf happens and an FTR is formed. The FTR's that are formed are decision points and areas of true supply/demand (where price often fakes out to gather orders for liquidity). The flag contains all the PA that exists within the flag limits. The Flag is the PAZ - the portion below and above the flag/PAZ are the flag limits which "box in" the area where price bounces around until it has the ability to engulf one of the two flag limits. These flag limits represent the furthest (most extreme) set of orders remaining. This is true supply/demand (within the context of the Flag it's currently in), and this is where the MPL's are located.

Fakeouts:

Here is a HTF chart showing a typical QM setup. I circled three critical areas that I will detail in future pictures.

More detailed:

My explanation:

These are good places to look for a low risk high return trade. I've noticed Salivan takes these frequently. I think the whole setup essentially revolves around two major pieces of PA: a fakeout followed by an engulf within the scope of a QM. For a bullish setup, we look on the higher time frames for a recent fakeout (to the downside) followed by an engulf into a PAZ (above). The fakeout forms the LL portion of the QM. The HH portion of the QM is the engulf into a PAZ above. This engulf is only valuable if it hasn't hit it's target yet. An engulf that hits it's target before retracing wouldn't be useful.

Let's go back to the fakeout for second....the fakeout is where all of the detail begins for the actual entry when price returns later on. I notice there are three areas that matter within the scope price forming a fakeout:

1. The decision point where price breaks down to form the fakeout (this is an FTR, a DP, and a FL). 2. The engulf of the DP to FO (price breaks the upper level of the FL that acted as the DP for price to EG) 3. The FL that forms as a result of the engulf of the previous FL that acted as the DP for price to fakeout. This new FL is the true demand and origin of the move up. It is within this FL that price will bounce on return. The lowest level of this FL is the MPL and price will often fakeout to this extreme set of orders. We can anticipate this by setting an entry order with a very tight stop loss. Nice R:R.

Salivan and IF both are confident in the trades they take...they have tight stops with large limits. They trade in the direction of an engulf that hasn't hit its target. Trading with such tight stops requires knowing exactly where the last extreme set of orders/liquidity lies within a FL. You are right to say that we should look for trades in areas where tricks were played in the past. In every one of Salivan's trades there is a fakeout that recently occurred and his entries occur near these fakeouts.

An analogy I think of: The fakeout is like a tornado that destroys a town and everyone in it. There is nothing good left for the survivors so most people pack up and leave town looking for a new place to live. A few people end up going back to this town a few days later in a last ditch effort to grab any money/gold/valuables left behind. Everyone left in such a hurry that inevitably there were some valuables left behind.These people gather up all the valuables they can find and hop on the last train leaving town. Salivan is always one of the people who go back to grab whatever valuables they can find

If the point of a fakeout is to grab liquidity by trapping traders into taking the wrong position and/or triggering stop loss orders, it would make sense that a fakeout would happen in an extreme area of a FL - the extreme opposite of the engulf and target. If this is true, we can conclude that fakeouts occur in an extreme part of a flag. If a fakeout takes all liquidity in its path, it would logically make sense that no orders would be left in the area where the fakeout occurred.

I have been spending a lot of time trying to understand the concept behind Salivan's deep retrace. It is confusing and complicated, but I think I might be starting to understand it. The deep retrace happens in a PAZ - between two FTR's which form the upper and lower limits of the PAZ. These FTR's also include FL's which act as the origin of the move down and the origin of the move up.

If you look at the chart, you will see the origin of the move down (also target for longs). Price falls from this level, and bounces briefly before faking out (labeled fakeout # 1) below the low of the swap zone confirmation FL Box (red rectangle) where new order flow was created. We identify the decision to fakeout, and wait for price to engulf this DP and form a FTR/FL. This FL/FTR is also the origin of the move up, and will be the target of future shorts (this is very important to remember).

Now that the origin of the move up/target for shorts is formed, we have a completed PAZ (the space between both of the origins). I labeled that in yellow.

Price continues up to the origin of the move down (like Salivan says, these origins act as magnets attracting price). When price reaches this origin, it creates another fakeout to the upside (labeled fakeout # 2). Wait for price to come back down and engulf to the downside (the engulf on the chart is labeled & occurs below the blue rectangle FL Box. This engulf is important because we know the target for that engulf is the origin of the move up (it has not been hit yet, so price will be attracted to it).

Price begins to fall towards the origin of the move up/ target for shorts but does not make it before reversing back to fakeout #2. Price is reversing to gather the remaining OF before continuing on to hit the target. This is good for us, because we will have a very tight stop loss and a wide target (as usual, we zoom in to find the DP to FO, and wait for an engulf of the DP to FO. The FTR/FL that forms after the EG is the best place to wait for an entry. In this case, the short was about 1:13 RR.

I don't know if I am 100% correct but hopefully someone will correct me if I am wrong. The hard part will be finding these live.... but with practice it will be possible.

I think the answer might be found in the swap zone that forms just prior to true supply/true demand.

Drawing:

1. FTR forms and Buyers are in control. Price bounces many times. 2. Price forms a RBD as it breaks the low of FTR 1. This is also the origin of the engulf 3. Engulf of 1 4. Price RT to DP to EG on its FTB 5. Price falls and a decision is made to break the low of the engulf (# 3) 6. New low is made

The last decision made (5) is the origin of the last move that makes the swap zone confirmed. Until a new low is made at 6, price could have kept rising. Instead, the sellers were in control when price tested the first DP...that test is the FTB (4). Sellers are too strong and push price down to form a new low (6). Now any RT to the origin of the new low is the final DP before the confirmation of the swap zone. It is where the first level of fresh sell orders lies - true supply.

Price won't fakeout above the true supply until it makes a decision to make a new swap zone. A fakeout above # 5 wouldn't net the IT's any more liquidity anyway as all the OF above # 5 was accumulated/distributed in order to form the bearish controlled swap zone. The first area where fresh order flow exists would be at #5.

Is this correct?

Here is a drawing, and a real life example:

At some point, the swap zone could itself be engulfed and a new swap zone could form. I think we are safe to trade the true supply in this zone so long as one of two things are happening:

1. Price has not yet hit the target of its engulf (in this case, the target for shorts) 2. The target for shorts is itself engulfed (target hit, but low extreme of the target is engulfed, indicating price wants lower...)

In this example, as long as there is a current valid bearish engulf (meaning an engulf with a target that has not been hit) we can feel safe trading the true supply area in the bear-controlled swap zone. Once the target for shorts is hit, and no downside engulf of this target occurs, we will wait to see where the new swap zone is formed.

Once a new swap zone is confirmed, we start the same process all over again.

I've been reading through Marketpedia and looking at my old posts, trying to conceptualize the MPL and true supply/demand.

We know FTR's and engulfs are everywhere on a chart...there are so many of them it would be overwhelming to draw each and every FTR/FL and engulf in every time frame on the chart. We know not every engulf and FTR/FL are created equal...some are much more important than others. We focus on the most important engulfs- specifically, engulfs of established swap zones.

If True supply/demand is formed after an engulf of an important swap zone, we know the true supply/demand level is also a FTR/FL. The MPL (as Jurij helped me understand with his post last night...refer to post # 953) is always located in a FTR.

If everything I've said is true so far, then it makes sense that not all MPL's are created equal - some are much stronger than others. The term "MPL" isn't inherently special in any way...it isn't a 'magic' area where price won't break. It is simply the most extreme set of order flow left in a FL. The MPL is only as strong as the FTR/FL in which it resides. Not all FTR's are important, and not all FTR's will bounce price. Some FTR's are weaker than others. Similarly, not every MPL is going to hold price the way we might want. There is no guarantee an MPL will hold price at any given time.

When price easily engulfs FL/FTR, it was able to break the MPL included within. Easy breaking of MPL = imbalance of order flow. Example - a FTR that forms after a bearish engulf that fails to hold price down doesn't have enough sell orders to compete against the buy orders that push price back up. The stronger a FL/FTR, the stronger its MPL will be. Strong MPL's will bounce price, and we can feel comfortable trading fakeouts to these MPL's.

If we find critical areas where an engulf of a swap zone occurs, we can be relatively confident that the resulting formation of a FL/FTR (and the MPL included within the FTR) will be strong. Strong FTR = MPL that is likely to bounce price. MPL's that bounce price have a lot of order flow ready to protect its position.

As always, I could be wrong, but I want to keep track of my thoughts.

I've been practicing lately on understanding scale. Here are some quick notes about my findings so far:

This is conceptual....I will be posting charts as I become more comfortable with the basics.

Price begins a new move by engulfing a swap zone. A FTR usually forms after an engulf and this zone is:

1. True supply/demand 2. FTR/FL 3. MPL 4. Origin of the move up/down 5. Target for future buys/sells

This is true regardless of the scale. 1 minute chart or monthly chart...the structure and fluidity of how price moves does not change. It is the dynamic behind how orders are filled and how price moves. PA doesn't exist because we say it does, or because we name the individual components. PA forms the formations we see because that is how price moves...

Analogy: we've all heard the comparison that the market is like a Russian 'nesting doll' (also referred to as Matryoshka Doll). It is a good analogy. Each smaller scale is nested in with the higher time frame that proceeds it. The higher the time frame, the more data is included (even if it is hard to see). We often have to drop down to lower time frames to see the details of PA on lower time frames. Every engulf/FTR/FL/PAZ/target/MPL etc.... exists in various scales within the market.

As with the market, each smaller doll fits inside of a bigger doll.

Assume all the dolls are put together: Even though you can't see all the individual dolls when they are assembled together, you know all the individual dolls exists within the largest doll. You also know (regardless of what size the doll is) the following:

1. Every doll has a head

2. Every doll has two eyes

3. Every doll has two arms

4. Every doll is painted and made of the same material etc...

5. ** You can't properly put the dolls all together without starting with the smallest doll and placing larger dolls over it consecutively. The entire doll's assemblage requires all dolls to work together** ( I am not suggesting you always start a top-down analysis by beginning on a 1-min chart, but I use this example to emphasize each part's contribution to the 'whole'. The smallest doll gets put away first, the largest doll gets assembled last (over the top of all the smaller dolls)

Similar to a Russian doll, the market has its version of heads, eyes, arms, etc...Each time new orders are transacted (regardless of scale), we have a new 'doll' with fresh order flow.

We know this following is also true:

1. Price engulfs to indicate future directional flow of price

2. FTR/FL formed after important engulfs are origins and future targets

3. Every engulf has a target - regardless of which scale it forms on

4. Engulfs are valid and important until its target is hit.

5. The MPL is important as last place of free order flow until price fakes out to consume the orders

6. You have to pay close attention to all time frames, at all times.

The smaller time frame targets have to be cleared before price can be free to move down and hit the original target for shorts - which originated at 'Bigger Doll A".

Once a target is hit, the engulf that preceded the target is satisfied, and price can move on to take out the next closest target... once that target is hit, price can drop to the next largest target etc... Price will satisfy all the lower time frame engulfs/targets first because they have to....these smaller targets/origins were formed inside the HTF PAZ.

I think this is how you can keep track of price on multiple time frames- know all of the EG's and Targets and identify them as they become satisfied. Always know where your main PAZ is located.

In order to know where to take a TT (virtually no stop loss) you have to know which engulf is in control (which 1-2-3 system is in control). As Salivan puts it, you have to ask "where is price coming from?" (at least this is my interpretation of why he asks this question.... I definitely could be wrong)

This is my greatest weakness - keeping track of where the most important EG (and its associated origin/target) in relation to the entire chart.

These origins and targets are important because they represent true supply/demand...which means they represent areas with free order flow. If we are going to take a trade, we have to know that there isn't any untapped area of free order flow opposite our entry (within our scale) or else, price will have a reason to take the order flow. I think this is why so many of my trades get stopped out...there is still free order flow existing in a pocket above/below my stop loss.

Assume this drawing is a HTF - Daily or weekly chart.

Assume the drawing starts with a downside engulf of a PAZ.

This is the "Biggest Doll":

System has three main points:

1. Engulf 2. RT to form Origin 3. Engulf has a Target

The PAZ is everything between the two FL's

The ultimate target for the engulf is to hit its target - which is the last HTF origin of the move up (at point # 3). Of course we know it isn't going to hit its target right away...a lot will happen in the PAZ. It may take weeks/months/years for the HTF target to actually get hit (depends on the time frame). Price is free to move around within the PAZ until it breaks one of the two FL's that establish the top and bottom of the PAZ.

Every engulf of a swap zone has the same '1-2-3 system' with its own engulf, RT to form Origin, and target for engulf. Imagine if there are 3,4,5 or 10 of these 'systems' all located within the largest time frame....it would get very confusing unless you had it labeled perfectly.

An engulf is only useful/valid/ if it's target is unmet.

This is a really long example, because I am going step by step for identifying the target. I don't think we spend enough time stressing the importance of finding targets

There are 12 charts posted total (over the next two posts) and it is step by step to show the phases of analysis. I hope this is organized enough to follow...if not, please don't hesitate to ask for clarifications

First chart shows the initial FL Boxes that got me interested in this area. FL Box C engulfs the low of FL Box A, and as a result, forms a swap zone.

Before analyzing the details of FL Box C to find a place to get short, I must find out where the target is located for this engulf. I need to find the target for shorts. I look left and see an area with lots of PA that exists before FL Box A. This is an area of consolidation where price eventually broke to the upside and formed FL Box A.

If I am looking for a target for shorts, I need to find the last opposing bullish controlled swap zone....

This next chart zooms in to this area (previously inside the neon colored circle in the chart above). Start drawing FL Boxes - only the important ones that held price AND as a result price made a new low/high. We only want the strongest zones. I found two main zones: the blue rectangle shows an area of bullish/buyer control, and the long black rectangle shows an area of very strong seller control.

Look how well price respects the upper level of the black rectangle....it takes a while to break this high. This is good - it means this is a strong bearish controlled zone. When price breaks this upper level, it will be significant.

When looking for a target for shorts, we want to find the swap zone that gives us true demand...remember on my previous posts I said "The best place to sell is in an area that is a target for longs".It works the other way too "The best place to buy is in an area that is also a target for sells". This true demand is the origin of the move up, and it is the 'magnet' that is attracting price from above. This 'magnet attraction' concept is something Salivan came up with and it makes a lot of sense.

Wait for the break of the strong bearish controlled rectangle. Here is when details matter...don't be sloppy/lazy with your analysis.

Just because price breaks the upper level of the strong bear-controlled rectangle (FL Box), doesn't mean it is the best place to draw your new Fl Box. Look for the following:

** Wait for price to break your important zone. After the break, label the breaks and the corresponding lows that form.

Look at these breaks and corresponding Lows: Pick the lowest low that forms and find the high that preceded the lowest low. These two points make up you new FL Box..the important Fl Box that holds the true demand and origin of the move up. You want to choose the high the corresponds to the last low that forms because you want to origin of the move up...it has to be the last demand zone before price moves up.

The chart below shows this new FL Box D. This Fl Box holds the origin of the move up.

Now..for the most important part of this whole example: As you can see in the chart below, price broke out of FL Box C and hit the target straightaway without returning to true supply. In a situation like this, you would want to be very careful about shorting at the FTB to true supply, because the engulf has already hit its target. Often times, I think failed trades are a result of not knowing where your target is located, after an engulf occurs. This becomes even more important when you start looking at higher time frames and drilling down on many different scales and time frames.

Getting in on a trade, in the right scale, because of an engulf that has an unmet target, will drastically increase the odds that your trade works out.

So which of these boxes represents the origin of the move down? Sometimes it is hard to know, but it is really important because origins are also future targets. Not knowing the future target means you don't know an ORFL when you see one. Not knowing a target/ORFL = not knowing if an engulf is valid and how far price may RT before hitting the target.

It can be hard to ID an origin, because often times there are multiple origins within different time scales.

What process do we use to identify an origin? Generally, they occur after an engulf of an important swap zone...but there has to more to it...especially when there are multiple engulfs of swap zones all located in close proximity together (as in this EUR-AUD example. It is easy to look back in hindsight and label origins and targets, because history gives us a complete view of price reaction. The difficulty is in identifying these origins/targets in real time. I would refine that statement by adding: the difficulty is in identifying the relevant origins/targets in real time, within the proper scale of the engulf you are using to begin your trade.

Every engulf has a target. Valid (actionable) engulfs have unmet targets

If every engulf has a target, we can safely assume there are many engulfs and many targets all existing in relatively close proximity to each other. How do we go about keeping it all straight?

Here are some of my ideas on this - I have been spending a lot of time on this question because I am convinced this is the key to success in trading.

Firstly: as intimidating as the issue of scale is, I think it is actually a major benefit to us traders...if we can learn how to use scale to improve and normalize our analysis. I am still very new to this, so I am also learning how to "use" scale to my benefit.

Scale offers us a chance to focus on one engulf/target at a time. LTF engulfs and targets will get satisfied first (by first, I mean the lower scale time frame engulfs/targets get met before HTF targets) This happens because PA is fractal, and in order for price to move long distances to satisfy a HTF target, it must pass through countless smaller zones full of LTF engulfs and targets. This is also where the PAZ concept comes in.

As confusing as the PAZ is, I think its intention is actually to simplify trading.

A PAZ is defined as the space between two FTR's/FL's. Regardless of the scale, a PAZ exists between two very important decision points (the areas of true supply and true demand exist within the FTR's that contain the PAZ. In order to break out of a PAZ, price must break through one of these important FTR's. Until this happens, price will bounce around within the PAZ.

How does price move out of a PAZ? I think it all goes back to FOF. Strong orders must exist to break previously important levels within a FTR. Strong orders means the bulls and bear fight it out, the team with the most liquidity wins.

Breaking a strong demand zone requires ample sell orders, and breaking a strong supply zone requires ample buy orders.

Fakeouts occur in areas of liquidity - usually to true supply/demand. A FO always has a specific purpose. Anytime we draw swap zones and identify the DP/origin where we expect price to react, we must be sure there are no remaining pockets of FOF remaining below our entry (or above our entry if we are attempting a short trade). A more clever question would be:"under what specific circumstances is a pocket of FOF located above/below our targeted entry relevant with regard to a potential FO?

Fakeouts aren't random - they are calculated moves to obtain liquidity. They occur all the time, but I don't think they are as random as they might seem (although I must admit they seem very random at times... )

Then there is the issue of reactive vs. original price action. Often times when we look at a chart like the USD-CHF example used in this posting, we see multiple lows and think they are all independently formed, when in reality they are often just a reaction off a different zone...it might be a reaction from a HTF area of true supply/demand but it also might just be a reaction of another reaction that is a reaction off a HTF area of true supply/demand.

To complicate this further, even in a situation where price is just reacting off a different level, the reaction itself is forming an independent true supply/demand level on a LTF chart. It is just in a different scale. So essentially, what we have is a whole bunch of reactions off other reactions that create new reactions. All these newly created reactions include smaller areas of true supply/demand (original supply/demand that is formed independent of any reaction) and within their smaller scales price will react to these levels accordingly. All of these originally formed areas of true supply/demand have their own MPL's which dictate how far price is likely to FO. How do we know which scales are relevant and which ones are not relevant when it comes to our trade setups? Again, I repeat the question I asked above: "under what specific circumstances is a pocket of FOF located above/below our targeted entry relevant with regard to a potential FO?

I think the answer to many of our failed trades can be found in answering these questions. We need to know which pockets of FOF (another way of saying this is "we need to know which areas of true supply/demand") are relevant to a possible FO occurring at our entry point.

Hi H, I see from your latest posts that you put in a lot of work and determination to understand the market and RTM. I also sense a bit of frustration which I totally understand. IMHO you are fine with market structure ie. identifying FL (true S/D) and FO vs eng.

The next part which helps to stick it all together is the psychology of ITs. In my opinion, we can't know which level is likely to hold unless we consider this, because ITs or smart money decides which level they want to sell/buy at. Remember we look for tricks into a zone where a trick was played. If there are no tricks on approach including manipulation of hope and fear then there's simply no trade because there are no signs a level is going to hold. Sometimes a level is fine to TT because of past tricks played at a zone which in itself is a very good place, for example an MPL or FTRFO within a FL aligned with a HTF QM level (FO/trick level), but then unless PA kicks in to let us hold that trade we must get out at first trouble area or cover enough for a possible stop as there are no clues for further IT intentions.

I'm no master at this, I lose too, but understanding this helps to filter out a lot of losing trades. Check the dissection thread, all setups have something in common, the manipulation of retailers (approach and/or history).

For example recent GU trade you took. It was a solid FL with CP on approach, could work and wasn't really a bad trade. The thing is the context of what happened before it. Price approached an origin and then engulfed up, after the eng up, price FO into the lowest possible QM in that zone and respected it with buying signs. Knowing this means a trick was played into a past trick zone (QM), so the intention of ITs are likely long than short although we have still a previous eng to the downside in play and price might still follow this but we also know the market doesn't move in straight lines and a RT is always possible. BTW when an origin is respected and an eng happens this is a big warning sign for a possible RT, independently of HTF engulf cycles.

Another aha moment I had recently was to not follow strictly the rules about higher/lower scale FL boxes and engulfs but instead trying to see the orders (true S/D) and the context in which they happen.

Something I have been noticing...I wonder if anyone else sees this too:

First, I think there is a difference between "true supply/demand (FOF) (origin up/down)" and the extreme end of a FTR that forms the edge of a FL Box. The True supply/demand doesn't always form in the FTR.

We draw Fl Boxes based on the break of swap levels, therefore we draw FL boxes based on the break of FTR's.

Example:

This becomes important when we look to ID an engulf....are we looking for an engulf of a FL Box or an engulf of the "true supply/demand/FOF/Origin up down" within the FL Box?

Both seem important...

So I started looking at areas of historical charts and I noticed some of the best reactions came from areas where there was an engulf of both the origin of a move up/down (FOF) and the top/bottom of its associated FL Box. Why is this especially important?

1. The engulf of a FL Box indicates an engulf of a swap zone (and the potential forming of a new opposing one) 2. An engulf of Origin up/down (FOF) indicates consumption of all opposing order flow, and newly executed FOF exists as a result.

We can draw lots of FL Boxes, but not every FL Box holds an important origin up/down. When an important FL Box (with an origin up/down located within it) is engulfed, the new zone formed is highly likely to react when price returns.

I've noticed an EG of the origin (FOF) is followed by a FTR, but it often turns into a confirmed FL once price continues on to break the extreme of the FL Box as well, and comes back to test the FTR. This ends up looking like a DP located just under a newly formed FL Box. The big bounce happens later on, when price returns to this area, and forms a FO to the 'DP' below the new FL Box (the DP is just the FL formed after engulfing the opposing origin. While the new FL Box is important to establish a new swap zone formation, the new FOF that is formed after the engulf of the opposing origin is where all the new orders exist. When they combine, the result is a very strong level with potential to bounce price quite far. (or at least this is what i have noticed recently, as always I could be wrong ).

In theory, this is a relatively easy concept to understand. The challenging part is executing the trade...

(assuming a short trade setup...it would be the exact opposite for a long trade setup)

The main components you must know for this trade:

1. Find an original true supply/demand zone with good history of price reaction (FL)

2. Watch for a FO above this level (RBD)

3. Draw the FL Box that forms as a result of the engulf of the original true supply zone

4. Draw the DP to FO

5. Draw the EG of the DP to FO

6. Determine the target for the EG of the DP to FO

7. If price returns to the newly created FOF (New TS) prior to hitting the target of the engulf, it is a high probability trade.

Making a mistake on any of the 7 main components above will probably result in a lost trade. I will be keeping track of all my losing trades to find out which of the 7 main steps I need the most practice on.

Hi Staurum

I have found that learning how to draw the FL Boxes has helped quite a bit when it comes to identifying engulf vs. fakeout. I used to open a chart and look for fakeouts and engulfs and try to piece together a trade from that perspective. Lately, I have been opening a fresh chart...usually in the middle time frame (hourly is good). I put everything else completely out of my mind..no thoughts about compression or engulfs or PAZ or fakeouts etc.... All I look for are areas where price was held down and I draw the FL Box responsible for holding down price. I do this until I have several levels drawn. When uncertainty arises I will refer to 4-hour or daily time frames. I usually look at the weekly time frame analysis too.. sometimes it helps to see the big picture when drawing the FL Boxes.

I avoid drawing any LTF FL Boxes at first.

Once have the HTF and middle time frame FL Boxes drawn, I begin to focus on other aspects of trading. Specifically, I start rating the FL Boxes according to their importance. How many times did they bounce price, were they formed as a result of an engulf of a very important zone? Was the FL formed after engulfing a ORFL?

With this focus, I identify two or three main FL Boxes that hold special importance and then drop down and look at the PA within the boxes. I draw the major swap zones inside the FL Box. I focus specifically on the three data points that make up a FL Box: the engulf, the RT/FTR, and the breakout (new HH or LL which confirms the FL Box). I find the origin and the fakeouts within the FL Boxes and make note of what levels they are a reaction to. Of course, the MPL is a critical part of this as well. I mark all the MPL's within the targeted FL Boxes.

Most recently, I have been focused on learning more about how these zones react with each other. How price moves from zone to zone...

I don't know the answer to this, but here is something I've been pondering for quite some time now.

I look at many successful trades where price reacts exactly as I predict, and my target is hit. Even in these trades, there are MPL's that haven't been hit above my entry. There is always a better level above/below an entry. We can't put a 500+ pip stop on every trade to account for the possibility that price will do some crap like this.

What I am coming to believe: The market is reasonably easy to predict if you have the right understanding of why price moves from level to level. I must admit, as unpopular as this viewpoint may be, I don't believe anyone can predict the market 100% of the time...even 90% of time. There are too many external factors that contribute to the global markets to say that there is a secret that will give us 90+ success rate in taking trades.

What I think RTM does best is teach a method to analyze the market in a way the cracks the code on how the algorithms work on the super computers that trade most of the IT's capital. The algorithms are predictable because they operate consistently...until they are adjusted/changed. There are so many big players in the market, sometimes an infusion of orders will enter the market and blow through setups that worked in the past. I don't think it is always our fault (sometimes it is) but it may be worth accepting there will be losses...our success depends on how we handle our losses. I don't think we spend enough time taking about this on RTM and it needs to change. All traders lose...and they lose on a regular basis. It his how they handle the losses that determines whether they are successful.

I do believe there is chaos (at times) in the market. There is unpredictability (at times) in the market. That is OK...we shouldn't try to over analyze why every trade goes against us. It is important to autopsy every loss to determine if there was a mistake in the analysis (this is critical) but it's OK to come to the conclusion that the trade failed...there isn't always a reason.

Once we can free ourselves from internalizing every loss as 'our fault' we can move past the losses and re focus our efforts on the next setup.

EUR-AUD is a good example...I should have been out after the ten pip loss. Instead I got back in and tried to get the next open level of FOF...which got blown through again and again and again. The trade I took yesterday has worked in the past (with regard to my analysis and execution). This time something else occurred, I was wrong, and that is OK.

If the market stops out a position, I need to accept it and move on. Tight stops, wide targets. Emotionless trading.

If I could sum up RTM and its concepts in a simple way I would say: RTM doesn't contain a special secret or 'holy grail' of trading. It teaches you to understand the market in such a way that you can get in to the market with very limited risk and very wide targets. In my opinion, this is the inherent beauty of the RTM forum and the education here. We trade at the best moments when FOF is likely to exist and reverse price.

It doesn't mean we are right all the time...and that is OK. I think it is a waste of time trying to be right 100% of the time. It is impossible.

With the right application and through hard work, RTM teaches a method of understanding PA in a way that ensures you will still be wildly successful...even if you are wrong half the time

Just my opinion, and I hope I didn't offend anyone!

The more I practice trading, the more I feel like the only truly important areas of PA are TS and TD.

Engulfs are worthless if you don't know which zone to focus on. FO is also worthless without context.

TS and TD gives us context...it is what helps us understand scale.

If I could offer one bit of advice to struggling traders...focus on drawing TS and TD. Everything else tends to fall in to place once you have the zones properly drawn in the correct scales. This is the advice i am giving myself.

Regardless of where price is traveling, it has to pass through many TS and TD zones along the way. The method for passing through these levels is the same regardless of scale. They are either engulfed straightway, or you have something that resembles a 1-2 test...all the important tricks tend to happen in these true zones with FOF.

Test 1 - at the SR of the TS or TD area. Supply/demand created on reaction and the trap is set for price to FO deeper in to the TS/TD zone at a later time. Test 2 - Price retraces deeper in to the zone and price turns. The trick is complete and the IT's have filled all the orders they need to hit the intended target.

I am amazed at how frequently this happens...so predictable once you see what's happening

A drawing I made this morning...

Is it the FTR that forms after the break of a new high that is important, or is it the decision to engulf that is important?

We focus on the FTR, but the FTR is FO'd all the time to the DP below...there are two scenarios I can think of:

1. The FTR that forms on the break of the high retraces down to the DP...so the DP is a tiny FL after it bounces price.

2. The FTR does not reach the DP to EG, and the DP is an FTR that price can FO to in the future. It is a trap being set.

This is an important concept because we want to predict possible FO, but it is also important when deciding whether an engulf has occured or not. Omid's drawing shows this exact situation...the DP located below the FTR that forms after the break of an important level. The FTB to this zone is a FO unless it breaks the low of the DP

If price visits the DP while forming a FTR, the break of the FTR is an engulf. If price does not reach the DP when the FTR forms, then we have to wait for price to break the low of the DP (not the low of the FTR) before determining if an engulf has happened.

Option 2: Getting out with no loss/minimal profit: Clearly, we can see that this was not the best setup for a reaction. With that said, as soon as price engulfed the MPL...GET OUT! There is almost always a decent RT after an MPL is broken. This is out chance to bail without taking a loss. In some cases we can even come out ahead by a couple of pips. The key: knowing the exact moment when your trade plan is shot and having the discipline to shut it down.

My # 1 motto for trading: I focus on capital preservation.

Option 3: Taking a loss. If price was allowed to run, it would have eventually stopped out. As we can see, the bounce at this FL was weak. Try to avoid this..be an active trader who manages their open positions. It will cut down on the losses. Imagine if you could control a majority of your losing trades at BE? All you would need is a couple winners from time to time and your account would grow exponentially.

It is important to review every losing trade...we need to know why the trade didn't work out. That said, the more I trade, the more I am convinced there is far more value in being able to contain the losses as opposed to bashing my head against the wall trying to find out what I did wrong. Sometimes the market does something we weren't anticipating...that is OK. I'd rather become an expert of slipping out of a losing trade at BE

One Idea i am experimenting with (to get out of a losing trade without taking a loss), is scaling in to the position.

If I get in on a trade at the SR of a FL (where we tend to see a supply/demand reaction), I can execute a trade of "X" size. Assuming the MPL of this FL is still fresh (orders remaining in the extreme end of the FTR) I can add a second entry order in this area. The size trade I place in the MPL will be approximately 3X the size of the first entry.

Here is my reasoning: When the MPL is engulfed we tend to see a RT back in to the FL. Sometimes the RT is not deep enough to cover the initial SR trade (especially if the FL is wide). To mitigate for this problem, I place a 3X trade almost at the edge of the zone. There is very little draw down on this trade, and if price does engulf the MPL, all it has to do is RT far enough to bring the second trade to BE, then travel 1/3 of the distance towards the first entry before the entire cumulative trade is net zero or slightly positive.

This dramatically increases the odds that I get out of trouble since I don;t need as deep of a RT to cancel out my first entry.

On the upside, if the MPL holds, the R:R will be incredible.

I have been pondering a new theory lately...nothing too spectacular...just been experimenting with session highs/lows. I know this strays away from the core RTM strategy, so if this is too off topic please let me know and I will delete the post.

I think session highs/lows are important to consider. Not because they hold significance based on theory...but they hold significance because many traders think of them as being important. They have all kinds of indicators that trade based on a break of a previous sessions high/low. Breakout traders love these trades..especially if the session high/low happens at round number. We want to trade where the herd's stop losses are located.

It makes logical sense to choose areas on the chart where the highest number of traders are likely to get caught on the wrong side of the trade.

What better place to look than at a FO of a session high or low? So many traders would get in on the breakout and get caught on the FO.

Here is an example: EUR-USD:

Red shading is NY green is London

1. LS that holds as the high of both the London AND NY Session. 2. LTF shows this as the first break and retest of the LS. This is the LS Kink.

3. The break above # 1 is a false break and many traders are caught trying to unload long positions. This is a RBD FO. 4. Price drops considerably making a new low 5. Price works its way back to the old Kink and there is a nice reaction that occurs at the FTR.

Note the downside engulf that forms just before the spike @ # 5

Here is another example on USD-CHF: same 1-5 labels.

I am trying to filter out weaker trade opps by thinking about "why" price reacts the way it does at certain levels.

It reminds me of high school math.

You can take and pass a calculus course relatively easily...by simply memorizing how to solve math problems. Math is systematic...it is exact and the process to solve the problems are well-defined and consistent. You can get an A in calculus by memorizing the steps. The harder part is understanding why...the application is the hard part.

So in terms of trading, I want to think about why price moves the way it does. Not just memorize terms and abbreviations and boxes. But understand the context behind what all of this means.

Price capping out at the London and NY session high is a good place to look for a FO but it isn't the only place. Any area of the charts where the herd is caught on the wrong side of a trade is a good place to look for a bounce/reaction.

So...after looking at the LS kink multiple time frames, it is clear that the range of the kink depends on the time frame. It would make sense to drop down to the lowest time frame possible to get the most accurate entry. I am finding that price does not always respect the LTF kinks...price will often times bounce somewhere within the larger time frame kink - often times just a few pips below the extreme low of the LTF kink. I think its good to find the exact entry, but equally important to give the trade enough room by placing a SL at the correct spot.

The problem with placing the stop wide enough to match the extreme low/high of the Kink, is it will usually hurt the RR. While I don't have the best answer for this, I think it is reasonable to simply wait for price to RT further in to the Kink before an entry is taken. This will inevitably result in many missed opportunities, but the trades that do occur will be amazing RR. The closer the entry is to the MPL of the Kink/FTR, the higher the return and the lower the risk.

So, it seems to me the following steps must be taken in order:

(for a bullish kink bounce)

1. Find a strong opposing FL that is broken. Mark low and high of the break. The high of the break is the UFL.

2. This UFL is the LS

3. Wait for this UFL (LS) to be broken to the upside. This break forms the head (RS)

4. Wait for price to RT to the LS line after breaking and forming the Head/RS.

5. We would expect a reaction at the LS (to fulfill the H&S pattern). Wait for this H&S to be ignored

6. Ignoring of the HS pattern creates a new high...this time breaking above the original LS and the Head/RS

7. Draw the Kink for the LS and prepare for price to return to this kink

8. We expect residual order flow to exist in this kink after price ignores the HS pattern, and we buy when price returns to this kink
